summary: Sorry for not completing, the idea was : Dustination tests whether NASA MERRA-2 dust data can warn of Saharan dust outbreaks before they start. We use daily dust aerosol optical depth (DUEXTTAU) over the Sahara and eastern Atlantic (25°W–20°E, 10–35°N), ideally from 2015 to 2025. An EOF/PCA analysis extracts the dominant spatial patterns of dust anomalies. A logistic regression then turns these patterns and regional dust levels into a daily probability that an extreme episode will begin within the next 1–3 days. Every model choice uses only the first 70% of the record. The final 30% is kept as a strictly time-ordered test, so no future information leaks into the forecast. We compare the model with two honest baselines, persistence and seasonal climatology, at the same alert rate. Skill is measured with the Peirce skill score and block-bootstrap confidence intervals. Dust outbreaks degrade air quality, aviation visibility and solar power, and affect health across West Africa and Southern Europe. A few days of warning could help with preparation. The pipeline is open, needs no extra toolboxes, and reports results only from real NASA data.
details: Our project explores whether hidden patterns in Earth's surface temperature variability can reveal potential early statistical signals of significant climate changes. Using NASA GISTEMP v4 temperature anomaly data, we developed a MATLAB-based approach that combines Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and statistical techniques to investigate long-term trends, regional differences, and changes in climate variability. By examining indicators such as autocorrelation and rolling variance, we aim to identify patterns that may not be visible through conventional temperature averages. Our approach emphasizes scientific reliability, reproducibility, and careful validation rather than making unverified predictions. Developed by a two-person team with AI-assisted coding support, the project demonstrates how publicly available NASA data can be transformed into meaningful climate insights using accessible computational tools. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to a better understanding of climate variability and provide a methodology that could be extended to other Earth system variables and, potentially, planetary atmospheres.
